item.title: China progresses plans for Mars sample return, asteroid flyby and more launch sites
item.dc:creator: Martin Smith
item.description:
As China integrates crewed and robotic missions to further its lunar exploration program, it is…

The post China progresses plans for Mars sample return, asteroid flyby and more launch sites appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
As China integrates crewed and robotic missions to further its lunar exploration program, it is also advancing plans to return the first samples collected from Mars. Closer to Earth, a student-led spacecraft is taking shape for a 2029 flyby of the near-Earth asteroid Apophis.

While investigating recent flight failures, China plans to further expand its spaceports, including support for an increase in sea launches.


Tianwen-3 mission

China’s Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission has entered the prototype development phase, with a number of scientific preparations underway, according to the project’s Chief Scientist and Chinese Academy of Sciences academician, Hou Zengqian.

The Tianwen-3 lander will drill up to two meters below the Martian surface. (Credit: CCTV)

The Tianwen-3 mission is currently targeting a 2028 launch aboard two Chang Zheng 5 vehicles, conducting sampling on the surface in 2030 and returning samples to Earth around 2031. The mission’s primary scientific goal is to search for traces of past life on Mars and could become the world’s first Mars sample return mission.

The project poses various technical challenges as well as scientific ones, as the team considers where and how to sample, methods of transferring the samples, and ensuring they do not become contaminated. The overall approach is reminiscent of NASA’s Mars Sample Return architecture shared in 2022, albeit without a rover pre-collecting samples from a wider range of locations.

A lander will drill for samples and load them into an onboard small launcher that will carry them to orbit. A robotic arm on the awaiting orbiter would then retrieve the samples and load them into a return capsule that will separate and return them to Earth.

The Tianwen-3 mission will launch samples to an awaiting orbiter and send them to Earth inside a capsule. (Credit: CCTV)

The process is far more daunting than lunar sampling, Hou noted, not least because Mars is significantly further away. The project aims to drill two meters into the surface to collect subsurface samples, which will be extremely difficult. Sampling from this depth better preserves the primordial information and minimizes impacts from surface radiation, oxidation and weathering on potential biosignatures.

Eight candidate landing sites have been selected, considering factors such as geological age, water history, habitability and the potential for obtaining around 500 grams of high-value scientific samples.

The project will benefit from the wealth of data collected by the Tianwen-1 orbiter over the last five years. The imagery from this orbiter is being collated into a global geological map of the red planet, similar to the maps of the Moon created from Chang’e imagery. This 1:5,000,000-scale map will combine high-resolution imagery, spectroscopy and other multimodal information and is expected to be completed before the end of 2028.

Samples will initially be analyzed in the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory in Anhui province, and later distributed more widely to scientists.

Chang’e 6 lunar samples presented to the United Nations for permanent display in Vienna. (Credit: CCTV)

Chinese lunar exploration program

China officially handed over samples from the Chang’e 6 mission to the lunar far side to the United Nations this month. The samples, collected in June 2024, will be exhibited on permanent display at the United Nations offices in Vienna.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) is now additionally overseeing uncrewed robotic lunar missions previously managed by the China National Space Administration (CNSA), starting with the Chang’e 7 mission. Personnel, resources, and knowledge are now being pooled together to benefit the Chinese Lunar Exploration Program.

The planned Chang’e 7 launch was delayed in August, following unfavorable local weather and, with unusually restrictive timing constraints, could no longer fly in its planned 2026 window. Its solar-powered lander and rover must reach the lunar south pole during a period of prolonged sunlight, while the low angle of the Sun must also provide suitable illumination for navigation and landing. Missing the tightly linked launch and landing windows has now pushed the mission to no earlier than early 2027, rather than simply delaying it by a few days or weeks.

A Chang Zheng 5 stands prepared to launch Chang’e 7 mission in August, which has since been delayed to 2027. (Credit: CMSA)

Learnings and hardware from the Chang’e missions will inform the design of future cargo landers, set to fly between 2031 and 2035. Unconfirmed rumors circulated this month around Chang’e 8 being cancelled, or its instruments being diverted to other earlier lunar missions, following comments by one team at September’s Europlanet Science Congress.

The mission had been designed to explore in-situ resource utilization near the lunar south pole, including experiments intended to demonstrate technologies for extracting and using local resources, such as turning lunar regolith into useful construction materials. It would work alongside Chang’e 7 to lay the groundwork for China’s planned International Lunar Research Station.

The mission attracted extensive international participation. CNSA selected 10 collaborative projects involving 11 countries and regions, with 200 kg of payload capacity made available to overseas partners. These include Pakistan’s first lunar rover and a Turkish exploration rover, alongside instruments and experiments from Russia, Italy, Thailand, Bahrain, Egypt, and Hong Kong – each of which has previously partnered on Chang’e missions. They are joined by experiments from Iran, South Africa, and Peru. Chang’e 8 is currently officially scheduled for launch around 2029, targeting the Leibnitz-Beta Plateau near the lunar south pole.

Rendering of Chang’e 8 on the Moon. (Credit: CNSA)

Elsewhere, Tsinghua University’s Student-led Threatening Asteroid Reconnaissance of Tsinghua (START) mission to intercept asteroid Apophis has now moved from review to the build stage. The 300 kg craft will launch in early 2028 aboard a ZhuQue-3, performing initial checkouts in LEO before raising its orbit to 31,600 km using low-cost solar electric propulsion.

The craft will perform a high-speed (8.74 km/s) flyby of the asteroid in April 2029 during its closest encounter with Earth, passing within 7 km of its target. Using high-cadence downlinks, imagery and data are expected to be returned within seven days.

Additional launch infrastructure

With Falcon 9 Starlink missions no longer flying from Florida, China launched more times than the Space Coast over the 30 days leading up to the publication of this article in mid-September. The count was still three short of the US total of 13 launches. As an increasing number of launch providers prepare newer vehicles for flight, or ramp up their cadence, China is planning even more launch infrastructure.

Proposed future pad layout in Wenchang from April 2025, with the third phase to the left. (Credit: CCTV)

The commercial spaceport in Wenchang is moving into a third phase of development, now that its third and fourth pads are near completion. The Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch Company (HICAL), which manages the site, plans a further four universal pads at the site during this next expansion. Commercial pads 3 and 4 could potentially host a launch before the year is out.

Work is also nearing completion on a third launch complex (LC-301) at the Wenchang Space Launch Site, with the shutter doors now attached to the two nearby vehicle assembly buildings. The pair will eventually house the two Chang Zheng 10 vehicles that will launch China’s crewed Mengzhou capsule and Lanyue lander for a lunar landing attempt before the end of the decade. While crew access arms are yet to be installed at LC-301, the pad is first expected to host the maiden launch of the single-core Chang Zheng 10A next year.

Meanwhile, iSpace is getting ready to start expanding its launch vehicle processing facilities at Wenchang next month, where it will work further on the company’s partially reusable Shuang Quxian-3 (Hyperbola-3).

HICAL is additionally planning to have completed the first of two planned droneships for offshore recovery of first stages by the end of the year. Capable of operating in ‘sea state 4’ (waves between 1.25 and 2.5 meters), the vessel is capable of 30 to 40 recovery missions per year with a roughly seven-day recovery cycle.

Orienspace’s Yinli 1 (Gravity 1) launches from Yellow Sea on Sept. 15. (Credit: Xinhua)

Increase in sea launches

China’s first sea launch took place over seven years ago in June 2019, when a Chang Zheng 11 (CZ-11) carried seven satellites to orbit from the Yellow Sea. Since then, 28 sea launches have been conducted, using the CZ-11 alongside CASC’s Jielong-3, Galactic Energy’s Gushenxing 1 (Ceres-1S) and Orienspace’s Yinli-1 (Gravity-1), which most recently launched on Sept. 16.

CAS Space now plans to perform the first sea-launch of its Lijian-1 (Kinetica-1) after trials in August aboard the Dongfang Hangtiangang ship in the South China Sea. The company envisages sea-launches offering customers more flexible target orbits, complementing monthly sun-synchronous missions from the inland Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center.

Construction began in late August to build a commercial sea spaceport in the Minhang District of Shanghai. Construction is estimated to take seven months, with sizeable vehicle storage and integration buildings alongside the Huangpu River. Vehicles would be transported from the spaceport using either the river or nearby canals to an offshore launch site. This new Shanghai Spaceport will begin sea launches in 2027, complementing the established Haiyang Oriental Spaceport in Shandong province, while another is being considered to the south in Guangdong.

Space Epoch’s Yuanxingzhe-1 prototype vehicle prepares for its sea-recovery test flight in May 2025. (Credit: Space Epoch)

Following Series B financing, Space Epoch’s Yuanxingzhe-1 reportedly targets a maiden flight before the end of the year, with commercial launches starting in 2027. Constructed in stainless steel, the vehicle measures 66 m high and 4.2 m in diameter. The company claims it could carry 14,000 kg to low-Earth orbit, 9,000 kg to a 1,100 km orbit when expended, and 7,000 kg when recovered.

Space Epoch successfully flew a vertical takeoff and vertical landing (VTVL) test with a prototype in May at the Oriental Spaceport in Shandong. The demonstration used a nearly 27 m test vehicle, which reached around 2.5 km altitude and was successfully recovered from the sea after a controlled splashdown for analysis. The forthcoming maiden flight would again target a controlled splashdown, which will inform future plans for catching later boosters using a recovery platform.

Galactic Energy showed plans earlier in the year to catch its Zhishenxing-2 (Pallas-2) using a tower with catch arms at sea. The company released new renders of that vehicle in single- and triple-core configurations this month, both featuring an interstage that implies it would utilize hot staging.

Pallas-1 launches on its maiden flight on Sept. 1. (Credit: Galactic Energy)

The company recently completed long-duration testing of its new-generation 100-ton-class Cangqiong-90 (CQ-90) engine. The CQ-90 burns liquid kerosene and oxygen using the gas generator cycle, and would power this new vehicle.

The company successfully conducted the maiden launch of its Zhishenxing-1 (Pallas-1) on Sept. 1 from a dedicated launch pad at Jiuquan. Galactic Energy intends to land and recover the boosters on future missions, once development has been completed on a throttleable version of the Cangqiong-50 engine.

Recent launch failures

A Chang Zheng 7A exploded just over a minute after launching from Wenchang in mid-August, carrying the ChinaSat 4B satellite. This, along with the fragmentation of a second Chang Zheng 6C second stage in orbit and other program delays, prompted the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) to issue a declaration that it faced a “severe quality situation” across its programs and that it has ordered more rigorous investigations and tighter quality control.

Tianlong-3 in the assembly building. (Credit: Space Pioneer)

Meanwhile, Space Pioneer’s review of the Tianlong-3 failure in April traced the anomaly to a liquid oxygen leak on the vehicle’s first stage, where a fire then developed. While both stages separated, this occurred at around 40 km in altitude rather than the intended 70 km. The second stage lost control shortly after ignition, ending the mission.

Nonetheless, the flight verified the majority of hardware items the company set out to test, it reported. The findings are being applied to a second vehicle, which could potentially launch in the final quarter of this year.

(Lead image: Landspace’s ZhuQue-3 seen lifting off during its second flight on Aug. 19, will carry the START spacecraft to orbit. Credit: Landspace)

 

The post China progresses plans for Mars sample return, asteroid flyby and more launch sites appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Starship’s upcoming missions: Waiting on Orbit, Building toward the Cape
item.dc:creator: Chris Bergin and Eleanor Day
item.description:
SpaceX is now targeting Starship Flight 14 no earlier than Monday, September 28, pending regulatory…

The post Starship’s upcoming missions: Waiting on Orbit, Building toward the Cape appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX is now targeting Starship Flight 14 no earlier than Monday, September 28, pending regulatory approval. The flight is planned as Starship’s first orbital mission.

If that flight goes well, Flight 15 becomes the first realistic opening for a ship catch and, in the best case, a double catch. Flight 16 remains the best-case first launch from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center, with this mission now internally cited as launching from 39A, according to KSC workers.

See Also

  • SpaceX Starship Program
  • L2 SpaceX Section
  • NSF Store
  • Click here to Join L2

After 13 suborbital tests, SpaceX intends to place Ship 41 into a sustained orbit at about 275 kilometers, complete roughly six revolutions over nearly 10 hours, deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and then deorbit for a splashdown in the Pacific west of Chile.

Super Heavy Booster 21 is not scheduled for a tower catch. Its job is boostback, a landing burn, and a controlled splashdown in the Gulf, with hardware and software changes meant to improve engine filtering and relight reliability after Flight 13.

Orbit, payload deployment, and a controlled reentry are the immediate gates, and later flights will be judged against those results.

Over on the East Coast, pad work at the Kennedy Space Center is already aligned with that sequence. The historic LC-39A was originally built in the 1960s for Saturn V, sent Apollo 4 off the pad in November 1967, and launched Apollo 11 on July 16, 1969. Twelve of the 13 Saturn V missions that flew used the LC-39 complex.

Saturn V (SA-511) launches Apollo 16 to the Moon from KSC 39A, April 16, 1972.#SaturnSaturday pic.twitter.com/9IxoIIU3hr

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) January 1, 2022

The same pad later supported 82 of 135 Space Shuttle flights before Atlantis closed the era in 2011.

NASA leased the site to SpaceX in 2014 via a deal brokered by Space Florida. Falcon 9 first flew from 39A on CRS-10 in February 2017, Falcon Heavy debuted there in 2018, and Crew Dragon Demo-2 returned crew launch to the pad on May 30, 2020. Starship is the next vehicle assigned to that historic launch site.

SpaceFromSpace / © 2026 Planet Labs PBC

Major construction at 39A now appears complete. The tank farm was active on three days this week, and on September 8 every major vent was in use as the farm stored, subcooled, and pumped LN2, LOX, and methane to the pad for testing and launch operations.

On the tower, the left chopstick actuator was removed September 1 and reinstalled September 10. Those actuators let the arms move independently for stacking and catching, and SpaceX’s newer chopsticks use electromechanical actuators rather than the hydraulic pistons on Pad 1, a change expected to improve response time and control.
The ship quick-disconnect arm also completed load testing later in the week. The SQD does not see chopstick-level loads, but it does carry the mass of propellant in the lines, so the test is meant to confirm the arm can hold that strain and take heavy side forces.

After the actuator went back in, the chopsticks were rotated and shifted, consistent with preparations for the first vehicles at the Cape.

On September 12, SpaceX opened 39A’s tower vent for the first time, a sign that chilldown of the ground support equipment feeding the ship, including the SQD and its umbilicals, is underway.

The vent also purges residual air and vapor from the lines after construction, when debris in the GSE or a vehicle is a launch-ending risk. Opening it is the clearest indication yet that 39A is moving from construction site to operational pad.

Separate from the pad itself, NSF’s Space Coast Live cameras recorded a Gigabay work stand and a ship horizontal-transport aft frame on a barge bound for Starbase. The frame is likely intended for the first Starship shipped from Texas to the Cape aboard the transport barge You’ll Thank Me Later, which now carries that name on its hull.
Flight 14 still needs a license and a clean countdown. Flight 15 still has to justify a catch attempt. A first launch from LC-39A by the end of 2026 remains a best-case path.

SpaceX will likely want to send Booster 22, caught on Flight 15, to KSC. If there are problems recovering Flight 15’s vehicle and they still intend Flight 16 to be Starship’s debut from Pad 39A, they could instead send a new booster to the East Coast.

Featured Image: Credit: Max Evans for NSF.

item.title: Progress MS-35 poised to launch cargo to ISS from Kazakhstan
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Day
item.description:
Following the departure of the Progress MS-33 cargo spacecraft from the International Space Station on…

The post Progress MS-35 poised to launch cargo to ISS from Kazakhstan appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
Following the departure of the Progress MS-33 cargo spacecraft from the International Space Station on Sept. 7, Progress MS-35 is expected to launch to the Station on Wednesday, Sept. 16. The cargo spacecraft will deliver pressurized and unpressurized cargo to the station that will sustain the current Expedition 75 crew.

Launch from Kazakhstan

A Soyuz 2.1b rocket will launch the Roscosmos Progress MS-35 cargo vehicle to the International Space Station (ISS) from Site 31/6 at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. The rocket is expected to launch on a northeasterly trajectory at 13:33 UTC during an instantaneous launch window. This is necessary for a launch to the ISS, as vehicles need to launch when the ISS’s orbital plane is aligned with the launch site. This allows the spacecraft to reach an orbit that matches the Station’s inclination, enabling a quicker, more efficient rendezvous.

Roscosmos delayed an earlier launch attempt on Sept. 9 due to issues with Soyuz’s third stage. The vehicle was rolled back to the assembly building and faulty parts were fixed before it returned to the pad for the current launch attempt.

The Progress MS-35 Soyuz 2.1b is assembled ahead of launch. (Credit: Roscosmos)

The Soyuz 2.1b vehicle is a three-stage, medium-lift rocket developed by Roscosmos. Four liquid-fueled RD-107A boosters surround the second “core” stage, which is powered by a single RD-108A engine. The third stage utilizes a single RD-0124 oxygen-rich staged-combustion engine. All three stages utilize kerosene (RP-1) and liquid oxygen (LOX) propellants.

See Also

  • Progress MS-35 Updates
  • ISS Section
  • NSF Store

Standing 46.3 m tall with a total liftoff thrust of 4,550 kilonewtons (kN), the Soyuz 2.1b vehicle can deliver up to 8,670 kg to low-Earth orbit (LEO). This mission will be the sixth Soyuz 2.1b launch of 2026 and the 105th overall.

The Progress MS-35 vehicle and mission

Roscosmos’s Progress MS-35 spacecraft will deliver 2,600 kg of cargo to the ISS. This will include pressurized cargo such as food, science supplies, and Station maintenance equipment. Alongside the pressurized goods will be items such as fuel that can be pumped directly into the Zvezda module’s propulsion system, potable water, and gases to replenish the onboard atmosphere.

The Progress MS-35 spacecraft has a total launch mass of 7,280 kg and can carry up to 2,600 kg of payload. The vehicle is 7.4 m long and has a diameter of 2.7 m. The spacecraft also has a 10.7-m solar array that, once unfurled, powers the vehicle.

Progress MS-35 during pre-launch processing. (Credit: Roscosmos)

Once Soyuz has placed the spacecraft in orbit, Progress will spend approximately 48 hours and complete 34 orbits to catch up to the Station. The vehicle is expected to dock to the ISS’s Poisk zenith port on Friday, Sept. 18, at 18:37 UTC. Progress will use the primary automated rendezvous system, Kurs-NA, to dock to the Station; however, the Teleoperator Control Mode (TORU) will also be available. TORU is a manual docking system that allows cosmonauts to dock a vehicle to the Station if the automated system fails.

The departure of Progress MS-33 from the ISS’s Poisk zenith port cleared the way for the new Russian cargo vehicle to launch. Progress MS-33 undocked from the Station on Sept. 7 at 18:27 UTC and destructively reentered Earth’s atmosphere, safely ending its mission. The spacecraft launched to the ISS on March 22 and spent roughly six months docked to the orbiting laboratory.

Render of current docked vehicles to the ISS prior to MS-35 launch (Credit: NASA)

Roscosmos first developed the Progress spacecraft in 1978. The original Progress 7K-TG vehicles supplied the LEO stations Salyut 6, Salyut 7, and Mir. The current Progress MS series has flown since 2015, resupplying the ISS alongside SpaceX’s Cargo Dragon vehicle. The launch of Progress MS-35 to the ISS will be the 188th overall flight of a Roscosmos Progress vehicle.

The current Expedition 75 crew is awaiting the launch of the NASA/SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the orbiting laboratory. The Crew-13 mission was originally scheduled to launch in mid-September; however, during routine pre-launch preparations, engineers discovered a leak in the spacecraft. SpaceX and NASA later announced that they had discovered an oxidizer leak and delayed the mission to perform additional testing and complete necessary reworks. A new launch date has not been publicly announced.

(Lead Image: Soyuz 2.1b atop Site 31/6 ahead of the April 2026 launch of Progress MS-34. Credit: Artem Pylaev)

item.title: Launch Preview: Nine orbital launches scheduled from sites around the world
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Day
item.description:
Nine orbital launches are scheduled worldwide this week. Two Falcon 9s are expected to deliver…

The post Launch Preview: Nine orbital launches scheduled from sites around the world appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
Nine orbital launches are scheduled worldwide this week. Two Falcon 9s are expected to deliver payloads from California, while a Vega C will launch Sentinel-3C & FLEX from French Guiana. Five launches from China are also on the manifest, including a Gravity 1 from Orienspace, and a Soyuz 2.1b will deliver the Progress MS-35 cargo vehicle to the International Space Station (ISS).

Vega C | Sentinel-3C & FLEX

The first launch of the week was on a Vega C, launched from the Ensemble de Lancement Vega (ELV) launch complex at the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana on Tuesday, Sept. 15. The medium-lift vehicle launched on a northerly trajectory at an instantaneous launch window at 01:21 UTC.

Vega C delivered two payloads developed by Thales Alenia Space to a Sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). This includes Sentinel-3C, a 1,143 kg Earth observation satellite developed by the European Space Agency (ESA) under the Copernicus program. The second payload, FLEX, also developed by ESA, will gather information about the health of the world’s plants.

The expendable vehicle features four stages and can deliver up to 2,300 kg to SSO. The first stage of the vehicle is a solid rocket motor, P120C, fueled by Hydroxyl-terminated polybutadiene (HTPB), ammonium perchlorate (AP), and aluminum powder (Al). The second and third stages, Zefiro 40 and Zefiro 9, are also solid rocket motors fueled by the same propellants. The fourth stage, the Attitude & Vernier Upper Module (AVUM), utilizes Unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine (UDMH) and dinitrogen tetroxide (N2O4) to deliver payloads to precise orbits.

ZhuQue-2E Block 2 | Unknown Payload

A ZhuQue-2E, developed by Landspace, launched from Site 96A at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on Sept. 15. The medium-lift launch vehicle flew on a southerly trajectory during a 22-minute launch window that began at 6:18 UTC, with liftoff at 06:26 UTC. The vehicle launched to polar orbit to deliver ten communications satellites for the SpaceSail Polar Group.

ZhuQue-2E is a two-stage launch vehicle that produces a total of 3,312 kilonewtons (kN) of thrust at liftoff. The first stage is powered by four TQ-12A gas-generator cycle engines fueled by methane (CH4) and liquid oxygen (LOX). The second stage uses a single TQ-15 engine, which is also fueled by the same propellants.

The launch was the third mission for a ZhuQue-2 in 2026 and ninth overall.

Gravity 1 | Unknown Payload

Gravity 1, developed by Orienspace, is expected to launch from the Haiyang offshore launch location at the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport in China on Sept. 15. The vehicle is expected to launch during a 21-minute launch window beginning at 09:50 UTC, with a planned liftoff time of 09:55 UTC. Gravity 1 will launch on a southerly trajectory to deliver an unknown payload to low-Earth orbit (LEO).

Gravity 1, a four-stage vehicle, launches from a sea-launch platform in the Yellow Sea. The vehicle utilizes seven solid-rocket boosters during ascent, with four igniting at liftoff, followed by activation of a core booster once the first four detach. The upper stages also use solid rocket propellants, and the vehicle has a total thrust of 5,880 kN at liftoff.

The mission will be the second launch of 2026 for Gravity 1 and the fourth overall for the vehicle.

Falcon 9 | USSF-259

The first SpaceX mission of the week is expected from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Tuesday, Sept. 15. The four-hour launch window opens at 6:00 PM PDT, with Falcon 9 launching on a southerly trajectory to deliver the classified USSF-25 payload to an unknown orbit for the U.S. Space Force.

Falcon 9’s first stage, B1097, will be on its 13th flight and will be recovered by SpaceX’s autonomous droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean. The mission will be the 720th overall launch for SpaceX, and the 106th Falcon 9 mission of the year.

Falcon 9 is vertical at pad 4E in California ahead of tonight’s launch of the USSF-259 mission → https://t.co/L2HTgohXdK pic.twitter.com/JwV3pf2D2m

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 15, 2026

Soyuz 2.1b | Progress MS-35

A Russian Soyuz 2.1b is scheduled to launch the Progress MS-35 mission from Site 31/6 at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan during an instantaneous launch window at 13:33:53 UTC on Sept. 16. The Soyuz vehicle will launch on a northeasterly trajectory to deliver the Progress MS-35 cargo vehicle to the International Space Station (ISS). Progress MS-35 will ultimately dock to the Poisk module on the Station’s Russian segment.

Soyuz 2.1b is a three-stage medium-lift launch vehicle that utilizes four strap-on RD-107A engines that wrap around the second ‘core stage’ powered by a single RD-108A engine fueled by kerosene (RP-1) and LOX. The third stage is powered by a single engine RD-0124 using the same propellants.

The mission will be the sixth Soyuz 2.1b mission of 2026 and the 105th mission overall.

Progress MS-35 during processing ahead of launch. (Credit: Roscosmos)

Chang Zheng 12 | Unknown Payload

A Chang Zheng 12 (CZ-12) will launch from Commercial Launch Complex 2 (LC-2) at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China on Thursday, Sept. 17. The vehicle will launch during a 29-minute launch window beginning at 12:25 UTC, with a planned liftoff time of 12:30 UTC. Chang Zheng 12 will launch on a southeasterly trajectory to deliver an unknown payload to an undisclosed orbit.

The two-stage medium-lift vehicle features a first stage powered by four YF-100K engines, fueled by RP-1 and LOX. The second stage utilizes two YF-115 engines also fueled by the same propellants. The 62-m vehicle can deliver up to 12,000 kg to LEO and has a total liftoff thrust of 5,000 kN.

Kuaizhou 11 | Unknown Payload

A Kuaizhou 11 is expected to launch from Site 95A at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on Sept. 17. The vehicle will launch on a southeasterly trajectory to an undisclosed orbit to deliver an unspecified payload during a 41-minute launch window beginning at 02:31 UTC, with a planned liftoff time of 02:35 UTC.

The four-stage Kuaizhou 11 is a 25.3-m tall vehicle capable of delivering up to 1,500 kg to LEO. The mission will be the third mission of 2026 and the seventh mission overall for Kuaizhou 11.

Kuaizhou 11 lifts off from Jiuquan. (Credit: CASIC)

Chang Zheng 2D | Unknown Payload

The final international launch of the week is a Chang Zheng 2D (CZ-2D), expected to liftoff from Launch Complex 9 (LC-9) at the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in China on Saturday, Sept. 19. The launch has a planned liftoff time of 10:50 UTC during a 23-minute launch window that begins at 10:43 UTC. The vehicle will launch on a southerly trajectory to deliver an unspecified payload to an unknown orbit.

The CZ-2D, developed by the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), is a two-stage medium-lift launch vehicle capable of delivering 3,500 kg to LEO. The first stage is powered by four YF-21C gas-generator-cycle engines fueled by UDMH and N2O4, while the second stage uses a single YF-24C engine fueled by the same propellants.

Falcon 9 | Starlink Group 15-27

The final launch of the week is a Falcon 9 expected to liftoff from SLC-4E at Vandenberg on Saturday, Sept. 19. The four-hour window begins at 6:47 PM PDT, with the vehicle launching on a southeasterly trajectory into a LEO inclined at 70 degrees. Falcon 9 will deliver 27 Starlink v2 Mini satellites as part of the company’s internet mega-constellation.

Falcon booster B1093, flying on its 17th mission, will support the mission, ultimately landing atop Of Course I Still Love You downrange in the Pacific Ocean after launch. The mission will be Falcon 9’s 690th launch and the 107th of the year. Furthermore, this mission will serve as the 225th orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026.

(Lead Image: Falcon 9 launch streak. Credit: Julia Bergeron for NSF)

The post Launch Preview: Nine orbital launches scheduled from sites around the world appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Ship 42 wraps chopsticks tests, Flight 14 moves to NET Sept. 22
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Day and Chris Bergin
item.description:
SpaceX has completed multi-day catch-related testing with unflown Ship 42 at Pad 2, then rolled…

The post Ship 42 wraps chopsticks tests, Flight 14 moves to NET Sept. 22 appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX has completed multi-day catch-related testing with unflown Ship 42 at Pad 2, then rolled the vehicle back to the production site for engine installation ahead of Massey’s static fire testing.

Flight 14 is now no earlier than September 22 in planning documentation, although SpaceX has not set an official target. That mission is not planned as a catch attempt, but a clean return for the Flight 14 vehicles could open the door to catches on Flight 15.

With Flight 14 hardware already through pre-flight testing, SpaceX has turned more of its Starbase attention to the next pair of vehicles: Ship 42 and Booster 22.

Ship 42 completed two cryogenic tests at Massey’s amid Booster 22’s own campaign, then returned to the production site before rolling back to Massey’s on September 9 for one more cryo test.
During these tests, SpaceX loads the vehicle with liquid nitrogen and liquid oxygen to simulate flight-like thermal conditions and pressures.

On the cryo stand, a thrust simulator also induces loads in the aft section as flight Raptor engines would when lit, verifying structural integrity under realistic temperatures and pressures.

Booster 22 left the production site on September 8 and joined Ship 42 at Massey’s. After a series of cryogenic proof tests, the booster rolled back to Mega Bay 1 on September 12 to prepare for engine installation ahead of static fire testing at Pad 2.

Booster 22 (Flight 15) is rolling out to Masseys for its initial round of cryogenic tests. @NASASpaceflight pic.twitter.com/UsDdNbjUHI

— Ceaser G (@CeaserG33) September 8, 2026

Ship 42 then made an unusual trip to the launch site well before it is ready to fly. On September 12, it was rolled into the chopsticks and lifted into what appeared to be a simulated catch position at the top of the Pad 2 tower.

Ship 42 is Flight 15 hardware, not the ship assigned to Flight 14, and it still lacked flight engines, pointing to a structural and interface test campaign.

In the hours that followed, the chopsticks’ pins and arms were worked against the vehicle, the chopsticks rotated west, and the ship was lowered to meet the quick disconnect arm.

Several small adjustments were then made to the ship’s position and the ship quick disconnect (SQD) plate to better align with the ship’s SQD port.

Today's Starship Ship 42 testing gave as a unique opportunity, as the @NASASpaceflight Starbase Live cameras captured the covers on the Ship Quick Disconnect plate being closed, as the arm moved away at the conclusion of that part of testing.https://t.co/1bbXAEmS9g pic.twitter.com/TAqbTJDyw9

— Elisar Priel (@ENNEPS) September 12, 2026

The likeliest purpose was to practice reconnecting the SQD arm to a caught ship so leftover propellant can be drained and the vehicle safed before it is moved away from the pad.

See Also

  • SpaceX Starship Program
  • L2 SpaceX Section

  • Click here to Join L2

After the SQD testing, the ship was raised back to the top of the tower and rotated back and forth. SpaceX kept it there for an extended period, perhaps to confirm the chopsticks could hold a ship if needed after a catch.

The rotations themselves were also notable. The sticks open widely to give a ship a larger target during catch, but last-minute corrections may still be required, and the ability to translate a caught vehicle provides margin if the ship is off-target.

Flight 8 offered a reminder of why that range of motion matters. After the chopsticks closed on Booster 15, the booster was swung to the north side of the pad for reasons that remain unclear.

Moving a vehicle already in the sticks is clearly treated as a necessity, even if that earlier example was a booster rather than a ship.

Once this testing was complete, Ship 42 was placed back on its stand and rolled to the production site Saturday night into Sunday morning to resume preflight operations, including engine installation. It will then return to Massey’s for a static fire.

The hum of the SPMTs, as Ship 42 heads back to the barn. The https://t.co/ddJvjEJLn1 pic.twitter.com/DAuaRMB0xc

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) September 13, 2026

Both Booster 22 and Ship 42 remain at least multiple weeks from flight readiness. Flight 14 is still next, now NET September 22, and it is not planned as a catch attempt.

If that mission goes well, Flight 15 could come on a much shorter cadence, possibly within a month, and could put the chopsticks work seen with Ship 42 into operational use.

item.title: Vega C set to launch the ESA Sentinel-3C and FLEX missions from Kourou
item.dc:creator: Justin Davenport
item.description:
Avio S.p.A., the Italian prime contractor, launch service provider, and launch operator for the Vega…

The post Vega C set to launch the ESA Sentinel-3C and FLEX missions from Kourou appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
Avio S.p.A., the Italian prime contractor, launch service provider, and launch operator for the Vega C light satellite launcher, is poised to fly the VV30 mission with the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-3C and FLEX spacecraft riding aboard a single Vega C rocket from the ELV launch pad at Kourou, French Guiana.

The launch is currently scheduled for 01:21 UTC on Tuesday, Sept. 15, with an instantaneous launch window.

The Vega C will take a northerly path after liftoff to place its payloads into a sun-synchronous orbit inclined 98.6 degrees to the Equator and around 810 km altitude. This orbit will enable the Sentinel-3C and FLEX payloads to observe the entire surface of the Earth, as well as passing over a given spot on our planet at the same local time daily.

The VV30 launch will last 116 minutes from liftoff to the final payload separation. Sentinel-3C will separate at T+ 1:00:49, just after the second ignition of the AVUM+ fourth stage at  T+55:28. FLEX will separate at T+1:56:03, and this will be followed by a fifth and final burn for stage disposal, in keeping with best practice for reducing the space debris hazard.

The Sentinel-3C satellite after unpacking at Kourou, French Guiana. (Credit: ESA/CNES/Avio)

The 1,143 kg Sentinel-3C satellite, the centerpiece of this mission, is one of four Sentinel-3 family earth observation satellites developed as part of ESA’s Copernicus Programme. The first two satellites, 3A and 3B, flew from Plesetsk Cosmodrome in Russia in 2016 and 2018, respectively, aboard Khrunichev Rockot launch vehicles based on the SS-19 ICBM.

Sentinel-3C and 3D will extend the original Sentinel-3 mission as the 3A and 3B satellites age out, carrying the Sentinel-3 program’s data record into the 2030s. The Sentinel-3 satellites are equipped with a common suite of instruments to observe Earth with various tools.

A sea and land surface temperature radiometer can measure global sea temperatures to within 0.3 degrees Celsius, measuring in the visible, near-infrared, and short-wave infrared portions of the electromagnetic spectrum. An ocean and land color instrument uses five cameras to provide a wide field of view, and is a medium-resolution imaging spectrometer capable of measuring in 21 bands from 400 nm to 1020 nm.

The FLEX satellite join with its launch adapter in Kourou, French Guiana. (Credit: ESA/CNES/Avio)

A synthetic aperture radar altimeter measures topography of bodies of ice and water, including sea ice, ice sheets, rivers, and lakes, with a 300 m resolution and a total range error of up to three centimeters. The radar instrument measures in the C and Ku bands and uses a microwave radiometer for atmospheric correction; it also uses Doppler orbitography and radio positioning integrated with a satellite receiver for orbital positioning.

The Sentinel-3 satellites also use a microwave radiometer to measure water vapor, thermal radiation emitted by the Earth, and cloud water content. These satellites also feature a laser retroreflector which not only provides an accurate orbital position of the spacecraft but also can obtain accurate topography of water features when used with other instruments. Finally, the Sentinel-3C is equipped with a global navigation satellite system receiver.

Sentinel-3C arrived at the launch site in July 2026, along with the Fluorescence Explorer (FLEX) payload manifested with it, and will be joined by Sentinel-3D in orbit in due course. But there is another payload on this mission also aligned with ESA’s environmental observation priorities.

The Sentinel-3C and FLEX payloads just before encapsulation in their protective fairing. (Credit: ESA-M. Pedoussaut)

The 397 kg FLEX satellite, like Sentinel-3C built by Thales Alenia Space, is equipped with the Floris fluorescence imaging spectrometer. This instrument will measure vegetation fluorescence on a global scale. When plants convert sunlight and carbon dioxide into oxygen, their photosynthetic activity is not visible to the naked eye, but is visible to the Floris instrument.

Scientists will use FLEX measurements to determine plant stress and health. These measurements will be used to determine plant photosynthesis effects on Earth’s carbon and water cycles. Together, the FLEX and Sentinel-3C missions will add to the  existing European portfolio of Earth science missions.

This flight is only the second for the Vega C program since Avio took full responsibility for Vega launch services from Arianespace. It is also the second Vega C launch of 2026, after the SMILE mission on May 18. The VV30 mission will be followed by the IRIDE Mission 2, Space Belt, and IRIDE Mission 1 flights, also currently scheduled to fly in 2026.

The Vega C program has a mixed record, with the Pleiades Neo 5 & 6 mission failing on Dec. 21, 2022. The last five Vega C missions, including the Sentinel-1C satellite, all succeeded, giving the rocket a record of seven successes in eight attempts to date.

(Lead image: The Vega VV30 mission at the launch pad. Credit: ESA – M. Pedoussaut)
